title: From Raster to Portal: Creating and Publishing an EBVCube
text:
Four dimensions, one file





EBVCubes use netCDF, a file format designed for multidimensional scientific data. The format keeps data values, their geographic and temporal coordinates, and descriptive metadata together in one self-describing file. It follows the Climate and Forecast (CF) and Attribute Convention for Data Discovery (ACDD) conventions, plus EBVCube-specific biodiversity terms. This common structure makes datasets easier to discover, interpret and exchange.
The figure uses the tutorial’s bird-diversity example to illustrate this structure. Each box represents one biological entity. It contains values on the same global grid, with time running along the depth axis.


Longitude (lon)
The east–west coordinate of the spatial grid. Its values are determined by the spatial extent and resolution of your data.


Latitude (lat)
The north–south coordinate of the spatial grid. Every layer added to the cube must use the same grid and coordinate reference system.


Time (time)
The date or dates represented by the data. The values declared in the metadata must match the layers you add to the cube.


Entity (entity)
The biological unit represented by the data: for example, a species, a group of species, or an ecosystem type.










Metrics and scenarios are not dimensions. They organise the four-dimensional data cubes inside an EBVCube.
A metric is what is measured, for example species richness, the relative change in species richness, or its uncertainty. Each metric group contains one four-dimensional data array named ebv_cube, with the dimensions lon, lat, time and entity.
A scenario is an optional higher-level group, normally used for projected data. For example, the same metric may be modelled under several alternative future land-use pathways. When scenarios are present, each metric is stored separately within each scenario: scenario_1/metric_1/ebv_cube.
If a dataset has 3 scenarios and 3 metrics, it therefore contains 9 scenario–metric combinations and 9 ebv_cube data arrays. All of these cubes use the same four-dimensional structure.

title: From Raster to Portal: Creating and Publishing an EBVCube
section: One real dataset, start to finish
text:
One real dataset, start to finish
This published dataset illustrates how an EBVCube stores several scenarios and metrics. The later units identify the exact example inputs used in their code; the same creation workflow can be applied to your own data.






Global trends in biodiversity (BES-SIM cSAR-iDiv)



id = 30 Community composition 3 entities 3 metrics 3 scenarios 1900 · 2015 · 2050
Bird species richness on a 1° global grid, modelled with cSAR-iDiv for all birds, forest birds and non-forest birds, under three SSP-RCP land-use scenarios. Roughly 3.3 MB, downloaded once and cached locally.
Martins, I., Pereira, H. (2022). Dataset page · DOI 10.25829/5zmy41

library(ebvcube)

ebv_download(id = 30, outputdir = tempdir(), overwrite = FALSE)

Keep this example in mind as you learn the workflow: its nine scenario–metric combinations show how several four-dimensional data cubes can coexist in one file. To create your own EBVCube, replace the example metadata and data where the units indicate. Your entities, metrics, scenarios, dimensions and metadata may differ.

title: From Raster to Portal: Creating and Publishing an EBVCube
text:
Before you start


You do not need prior knowledge of EBVs, netCDF files or the EBV Data Portal. Unit 1 introduces the concepts and vocabulary used throughout the tutorial.
It helps to be comfortable with:

basic R: installing packages and running scripts;
basic geospatial data handling in R, using packages such as terra;
biodiversity raster data, if you want to create your own EBVCube rather than follow the example.

A free GEO BON account is needed if you use the portal’s metadata form or submit a dataset for publication. It is not needed to read public datasets or follow the R-only metadata workflow.


Key resources

EBV Data Portal — discover, download and publish EBV datasets.
ebvcube on GitHub — also on CRAN and the b-cubed r-universe.
Package documentation — the full function reference this tutorial builds on.
Format specification — the structural rules behind the format.
GEO BON — what are EBVs? — the canonical definition and the six classes.
Quoss et al. (2022) — the methods paper describing the package.
crumbs: Overview

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 What is an Essential Biodiversity Variable?
An Essential Biodiversity Variable (EBV) is a standardised measurement of an important aspect of biodiversity. EBVs provide a common language for describing and tracking biodiversity change across places and time. They can be derived from field observations, remote sensing, or models, and sit between those primary sources and the indicators used for assessment, reporting, and decision making (Group on Earth Observations Biodiversity Observation Network, n.d.; Pereira et al., 2013).
An EBV is not a file. An EBVCube is the standardised file used to store gridded EBV data, together with the information needed to interpret it. Think of the EBV framework as the shared language for biodiversity measurements, and the EBVCube as one way to make those measurements consistent, reusable, and comparable.
crumbs: 1  Introduction

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 The six EBV classes
EBVs are organised into six classes, each capturing a different dimension of biodiversity:


Genetic composition
Genetic diversity and differentiation within and among populations.


Species populations
Where species occur and how abundant they are.


Species traits
Physical, physiological and behavioural characteristics of organisms.


Community composition tutorial example
The diversity and mix of species within a community.


Ecosystem structure
The physical build and extent of ecosystems.


Ecosystem function
The processes and productivity that keep ecosystems running.


The dataset we use throughout this tutorial, Global trends in biodiversity (BES-SIM cSAR-iDiv), belongs to the Community composition class.






Canonical classes vs. what you see on the portal





The six classes above are the canonical classification defined by GEO BON. On the EBV Data Portal, you may not see all six at once, because the portal lists only the classes represented by available datasets. The portal may also show additional catalogue labels; these do not replace the six canonical EBV classes.
Ecosystem services is not one of the six EBV classes. It belongs to a separate, complementary GEO BON framework, the Essential Ecosystem Service Variables (EESVs), which covers the benefits people obtain from nature rather than biodiversity itself. For the official classification, see the GEO BON definitions page.
crumbs: 1  Introduction

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.3 Why netCDF? The EBVCube format
An EBVCube is designed for gridded biodiversity data: values arranged across geographic space and, often, through time. Storing each map or time step as a separate file quickly becomes difficult to manage and interpret. The Network Common Data Form (netCDF), long used in the climate sciences, keeps the data and the information that explains it together in one self-describing file: units, dates, entities, and coordinate reference system travel with the values.
The EBVCube is the standardised, netCDF-based data format defined for EBVs. It follows two established conventions: CF v1.8 (Eaton et al., 2020), which defines how coordinates, units, and time are encoded; and ACDD v1.3 (Earth Science Information Partners, 2015), which defines metadata that makes a dataset easier to discover and understand. EBVCube-specific biodiversity terms complete the format (Quoss et al., 2024).
Every data cube inside an EBVCube shares the same four dimensions. Together, they locate each data value: where, when, and for which biological entity.


Longitude (lon)
The east–west coordinate of the grid, or the projected x-coordinate.


Latitude (lat)
The north–south coordinate of the grid, or the projected y-coordinate.


Time (time)
One date or a whole series: annual, decadal, scenario years, irregular.


Entity (entity)
The biological unit: a species, a group of species, or an ecosystem type.


The entity dimension lets one EBVCube hold data for many species or other biological units at once. Above these four dimensions, metrics and scenarios organise the data cubes inside the file. A metric is what is measured, such as species richness or its uncertainty. A scenario is an optional grouping, normally used for projected data under alternative future pathways.
Our example uses both levels: three scenarios, each with three metrics, make nine data cubes in total. Every one uses the same four dimensions. We return to this hierarchy in Unit 4.






Figure 1.1: Overview of the EBVCube data model. An EBV dataset combines a hierarchical structure of scenarios and metrics with four-dimensional data cubes (longitude, latitude, time, and entity), and carries standardised metadata following the CF 1.8, ACDD 1.3, and EBV conventions. Source: Quoß et al. (in preparation).
crumbs: 1  Introduction

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.4 Touring the EBV Data Portal
Published EBV datasets can be found on the EBV Data Portal. Throughout this tutorial we use one of them as the running example:






Worked example: Global trends in biodiversity (BES-SIM cSAR-iDiv)
id = 30 Community composition DOI 10.25829/5zmy41
Martins, I., Pereira, H. (2022). Global trends in biodiversity (BES-SIM cSAR-iDiv) (Version 1) [Dataset]. German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research (iDiv) Halle-Jena-Leipzig. DOI 10.25829/5zmy41 (Martins & Pereira, 2022)
We picked this dataset deliberately. It reports bird species richness for 1900, 2015 and 2050 across three entities (all birds, forest birds, non-forest birds), under three SSP×RCP land-use scenarios. Because it carries both a scenario level and multiple metrics, working through it exposes the entire EBVCube hierarchy — a dataset without scenarios would let you finish the tutorial without ever meeting half the structure.



Open the dataset page and you will find information that supports FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable) use of the dataset:

a stable dataset ID (30) and a persistent DOI you can cite;
a structured JSON metadata record (title, abstract, EBV class, creators, license, entities);
the netCDF file itself, available for direct download (≈ 3.3 MB);
an interactive EBV Visualizer for exploring maps and temporal trends without downloading anything.

The three views you will use most are the Discover page (Figure 1.2), an individual dataset page, and the live EBV Visualizer. Click the Discover screenshot to enlarge it.

Discover pageDataset pageEBV Visualizer








Figure 1.2: The Discover page showing the EBV class filters and a list of datasets.





Open dataset id = 30 on the EBV Data Portal to inspect its general metadata, entities, citation, DOI, and netCDF download. 













Portal interface checked in August 2026. The portal is updated from time to time, so small layout differences are normal; the metadata, DOI, and download remain on the dataset page.



Browsing and inspecting datasets like this is how you find data on the portal. Next, we look at how you work with it.
crumbs: 1  Introduction

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.5 Where ebvcube fits
The portal is where EBV data is published and discovered. The ebvcube R package (Quoß et al., 2022; Quoss et al., 2024) lets you discover, access, visualise, and create EBVCubes.


DISCOVER
Inspect a published file
Find out what a file contains and how it is organised: list its data-cube paths and inspect its metadata before reading any values.


ACCESS
Read the data you need
Download a published file, read a selected entity or time step, or subset it to a geographic area instead of loading more data than you need.


VISUALISE
Explore patterns and change
Make a map of one data slice or a trend plot through time, without first learning the details of netCDF.


CREATE
Producing new data
Starting from your own rasters or model output, ebvcube assembles them into a valid EBVCube, ready to upload and publish on the portal with its own DOI.


This tutorial concentrates on the path from understanding a published dataset to creating and publishing your own EBVCube, one step at a time.






Checkpoint. Open dataset id = 30 on the portal and identify its EBV class, DOI, entities, and the file formats offered for download. Then identify one scenario and one metric in the dataset. If you can also explain why the data is stored as netCDF rather than as a folder of maps, you are ready to install the software in Unit 2.







Earth Science Information Partners. (2015). Attribute Convention for Data Discovery (ACDD), Version 1.3. https://wiki.esipfed.org/Attribute_Convention_for_Data_Discovery_1-3. https://wiki.esipfed.org/Attribute_Convention_for_Data_Discovery_1-3


Eaton, B., Gregory, J., Drach, B., Taylor, K., Hankin, S., et al. (2020). NetCDF Climate and Forecast (CF) Metadata Conventions, Version 1.8. https://cfconventions.org/. https://cfconventions.org/Data/cf-conventions/cf-conventions-1.8/cf-conventions.html


Group on Earth Observations Biodiversity Observation Network. (n.d.). GEO BON. https://geobon.org/. Retrieved July 31, 2026, from https://geobon.org/


Martins, I., & Pereira, H. M. (2022). Global trends in biodiversity (BES-SIM cSAR-iDiv) (Version 1). Dataset, EBV Data Portal; German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research (iDiv) Halle-Jena-Leipzig. https://doi.org/10.25829/5zmy41


Pereira, H. M., Ferrier, S., Walters, M., Geller, G. N., Jongman, R. H., Scholes, R. J., Bruford, M. W., Brummitt, N., Butchart, S. H., Cardoso, A., et al. (2013). Essential biodiversity variables. Science, 339(6117), 277–278.


Quoss, L., Fernandez, N., Langer, C., Valdez, J., & Pereira, H. M. (2024). Ebvcube: Working with netCDF for essential biodiversity variables. German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research (iDiv) Halle-Jena-Leipzig. https://github.com/EBVcube/ebvcube


Quoß, L., Fernández, N., Langer, C., Valdez, J., Fernández, M. A., & Pereira, H. M. (2022). Building essential biodiversity variable netCDFs with the ebvcube r package. Biodiversity Information Science and Standards, 6, e91215. https://doi.org/10.3897/biss.6.91215

title: 2  Installing software and the ebvcube R package
text:
R ≥ 4.2.0 required
The minimum version ebvcube supports. Check yours with R.version.string, and if it is older, update R first, or CRAN will refuse to install the package.


RStudio recommended
A free, widely used editor for R. It is not required, but it makes it easier to run, save, and revisit the code in this tutorial. Download it here.








What about HDF5 and GDAL?





On Windows and macOS, you will usually not need to install HDF5 or GDAL yourself. Bioconductor supplies HDF5 through rhdf5, while CRAN binary builds of terra normally include the spatial libraries they need. Linux installations can require additional system libraries; Unit 7 covers the common fixes.
crumbs: 2  Installing software and the `ebvcube` R package

title: 2  Installing software and the ebvcube R package
text:
2.2 Installing ebvcube from CRAN
For most users, the released version on CRAN is all you need:

install.packages("ebvcube")

CRAN resolves all of the CRAN dependencies automatically. Three dependencies, however, live on Bioconductor rather than CRAN, so on a fresh machine you will usually need the one-time step in the next section as well.






Other ways to install





Most people should use CRAN. If you need a newer feature, you can install the development version with devtools::install_github("EBVcube/ebvcube", ref = "dev"), or get the binary builds from the b-cubed r-universe. These are covered in the package’s installation guide.
crumbs: 2  Installing software and the `ebvcube` R package

title: 2  Installing software and the ebvcube R package
text:
2.3 Adding the Bioconductor dependencies
Three of ebvcube’s dependencies come from Bioconductor rather than CRAN, because reading EBVCube files means reading HDF5 under the hood:


rhdf5
Low-level HDF5 read/write, since netCDF-4 is HDF5 underneath.


DelayedArray
Lazy, on-disk arrays so large cubes do not exhaust your RAM.


HDF5Array
Connects DelayedArray to HDF5 files.


If installing ebvcube reports that one of these is missing, install them with BiocManager:

install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install(c("rhdf5", "DelayedArray", "HDF5Array"))

You only need to do this once per R installation.






Which Bioconductor version?





BiocManager automatically selects the Bioconductor release that matches your version of R. Leave the version unspecified unless a package maintainer or a project requirement tells you otherwise.
crumbs: 2  Installing software and the `ebvcube` R package

title: 2  Installing software and the ebvcube R package
text:
2.4 Verifying your installation
First, load the package and confirm the version:

library(ebvcube)
packageVersion("ebvcube")

Then open the small example dataset that ships with the package. Because it is bundled, this needs no download and works offline, making it a reliable installation check:

file <- system.file("extdata", "martins_comcom_subset.nc", package = "ebvcube")

prop <- ebv_properties(file, verbose = FALSE)
prop@general$title
#> [1] "Local bird diversity (cSAR/BES-SIM)"







Why is the test file different from the tutorial example?





They are two different published datasets, which can be easy to miss.
The file bundled inside ebvcube is a spatial subset of Local bird diversity (cSAR/BES-SIM), portal id = 1. The dataset this tutorial follows is Global trends in biodiversity (BES-SIM cSAR-iDiv), portal id = 30. They share a lead author and a model family, which is why the names look so similar, but they are separate published products: id = 1 covers 1900–2015 with no scenarios, while id = 30 covers 1900, 2015 and 2050 across three SSP×RCP scenarios.
We use the bundled file here and only here, because verifying an installation should not depend on a working internet connection. The tutorial’s scenario-based reference dataset is id = 30.



If the title prints, your installation is working. You can then optionally download the tutorial’s scenario-based reference dataset from the portal (≈ 3.3 MB). This second check requires an internet connection:

file <- ebv_download(id = 30, outputdir = tempdir(), overwrite = FALSE)
prop <- ebv_properties(file, verbose = FALSE)
prop@general$title
#> [1] "Global trends in biodiversity (BES-SIM cSAR-iDiv)"







Checkpoint. Your setup is complete when library(ebvcube) loads without error and ebv_properties() prints the title of the bundled dataset. Downloading id = 30 is an optional connectivity check. Once the installation check works, you are ready to prepare biodiversity data in Unit 3.
crumbs: 2  Installing software and the `ebvcube` R package

title: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata
text:
3.1 Inspect the structure of a published EBVCube
Start by inspecting the structure of dataset id = 30, the published EBVCube used throughout this tutorial. The dataset contains three scenarios and three metrics. Since each scenario–metric combination is stored as a separate data cube, we expect the file to contain nine data cubes.
# Load library 
library(ebvcube)
# Download dataset with id=30
file <- ebv_download(id = 30, outputdir = tempdir(), overwrite = FALSE)
# Get data cubes paths
paths <- ebv_datacubepaths(file, verbose = FALSE)
nrow(paths)
#> [1] 9
paths
The result confirms that the file contains nine data cubes. Each scenario–metric combination has its own path, for example scenario_1/metric_1/ebv_cube.
crumbs: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata

title: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata
text:
Why inspect the structure first?



Functions such as ebv_datacubepaths() let you understand how a published EBVCube is organised before reading its values. This is useful when deciding which scenario, metric, time step, or entity you want to access.
crumbs: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata

title: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata
section: 3.2 What you need before creating an EBVCube
text:
3.2 What you need before creating an EBVCube
Before creating an EBVCube, you need to define its structure and prepare the data that will populate it. ebv_create() uses the information you provide; it does not infer the intended structure from the input rasters. Four components therefore need to be prepared:


A metadata JSON
Describes the dataset and its hierarchy, including the title, creators, licence, EBV class, metrics, and scenarios. You can create it through the EBV Data Portal or, optionally, with ebv_metadata().


Data values
The spatial values that will populate the data cubes. These can come from individual raster layers or from multiple time steps stored in multi-band GeoTIFFs.


Entity names
The biological units represented in the data, provided in a fixed order. In dataset id = 30, these are All birds, Forest birds, and Non-forest birds.


Creation settings
The coordinate reference system, spatial extent, resolution, exact time steps, and no-data value used to define the dimensions of the EBVCube. You provide these to ebv_create() in Unit 4.








Coverage and exact time steps are different



The metadata JSON describes the dataset’s temporal coverage, for example 1900–2050. The exact time steps stored in the EBVCube, such as 1900, 2015, and 2050, are provided separately through ebv_create(timesteps = ...) in Unit 4.
The same principle applies to space: the metadata describes the dataset’s spatial coverage, while ebv_create() receives the exact coordinate reference system, extent, and resolution used to construct the grid.
crumbs: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata

title: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata
section: 3.3 Data cubes and spatial layers are not the same
text:
3.3 Data cubes and spatial layers are not the same
Dataset id = 30 illustrates an important distinction between the number of data cubes in an EBVCube and the number of two-dimensional spatial layers needed to populate them.








In dataset id = 30
Calculation
Result




Data cubes
3 scenarios × 3 metrics
9


Two-dimensional map layers
3 entities × 3 dates × 3 scenarios × 3 metrics
81



Each of the nine data cubes has four dimensions: longitude, latitude, time, and entity. With three entities and three dates, each cube contains nine two-dimensional spatial slices. Across nine cubes, this gives 81 spatial slices.
These slices do not necessarily correspond to 81 separate files. For example, several time steps can be stored together in a multi-band GeoTIFF.
The key distinction is therefore:

scenarios × metrics determines the number of data cubes;
entities × dates × scenarios × metrics determines the number of spatial slices needed to populate them.
crumbs: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata

title: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata
text:
## Prepare your own data
If you are following the published example, use this section as a checklist for later. If you are working with your own biodiversity data, check these points before continuing to Unit 4.


One shared grid
Every layer has the same coordinate reference system, extent, and resolution.


Complete data coverage
You can account for every combination of entity, time step, metric, and scenario that the EBVCube will contain.


Final entity names
One name per entity, in the same order in your metadata and data layers.


Exact creation settings
You know the EPSG code, extent, resolution, time steps, and fill value you will pass to ebv_create().


Consistent source data
Your GeoTIFFs or in-memory rasters load correctly, use the expected grid, and represent missing values consistently.








Check a folder of GeoTIFFs






# Install and/or load library
install.package('terra')
library(terra)

# List all the GeoTIFFs from your folder
layers <- rast(list.files("path/to/your/tifs", pattern = "\\.tif$",
                          full.names = TRUE))
layers  # inspect extent, resolution, CRS, and number of layers

Use this only with your own data. It is a quick first check, not a replacement for checking that each layer has the intended entity, date, metric, and scenario.
crumbs: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata

title: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata
text:
3.4 Create the metadata JSON
Every EBVCube is created from a metadata JSON that describes the dataset and its scenario–metric hierarchy. There are two ways to create it. The EBV Data Portal - is the recommended route since its form guides you through the required fields and controlled vocabularies. Alternatively, ebv_metadata() allows you to generate the metadata in R.

3.4.1 Path A — EBV Data Portal
Open Uploads → New Upload in the EBV Data Portal. Complete the required fields in the first two tabs, then use the third tab to generate and download the metadata JSON.

General informationGeneral informationEBV attributesData upload





Add the title, creation date, summary, methods, creators, licence, and related DOIs, among other general information.






Figure 3.1: New upload — General information.





Choose the EBV class, EBV name, and entity type from the portal’s fixed lists. Add the metrics, including their names, descriptions, and units. Add scenarios when the same metrics occur under alternative projected pathways.






Figure 3.2: New upload — EBV attributes.





Click Download Metadata to save the .json file. This is the file you pass to ebv_create() in Unit 4. You return to this tab later to upload the finished netCDF.






Figure 3.3: New upload — Data upload, with the Download Metadata link.












A GEO BON account is required



You need a GEO BON account at members.geobon.org to access the upload workflow, create and download the metadata JSON, and later submit the completed EBVCube through the EBV Data Portal.




3.4.2 Path B — R with ebv_metadata()
Use ebv_metadata() when you want to generate metadata programmatically. The example below uses dataset id = 30 to illustrate how the same type of metadata can be defined in R. It is intended as a learning example; replace all dataset-specific information when creating an EBVCube from your own data.






Create an id = 30-style metadata JSON






json <- ebv_metadata(
  outputpath            = file.path(tempdir(), "metadata.json"),
  title                 = "Global trends in biodiversity (BES-SIM cSAR-iDiv)",
  summary               = "Projections from the cSAR-iDiv model from 1900 to 2050 using LUH2 and SSP-RCP pathways for the BES-SIM inter-model comparison.",
  references            = "10.1126/science.adn3441",
  source                = "cSAR-iDiv model team, 14 December 2018",
  project_name          = "BES-SIM",
  project_url           = "https://ipbes.net/scenarios-models/expert-group-activities",
  date_created          = "2022-03-21",
  creator_name          = "Inês Martins",
  creator_institution   = "German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research (iDiv)",
  contributor_name      = "Henrique M. Pereira",
  license               = "CC BY",
  ebv_class             = "Community composition",
  ebv_name              = "Taxonomic and phylogenetic diversity",
  ebv_spatial_scope     = "Global",
  ebv_domain            = "Terrestrial",
  coverage_content_type = "modelResult",
  ebv_entity_type       = "Communities",
  ebv_entity_scope      = "Bird species (forest and non-forest)",
  time_coverage_start      = "1900-01-01",
  time_coverage_end        = "2050-01-01",
  time_coverage_resolution = "Irregular",
  ebv_scenario_classification_name    = "SSP-RCP",
  ebv_scenario_classification_version = "LUH2, CMIP5/ISIMIP2a",
  metric = list(
    list(standard_name = "Species richness (S)",
         long_name     = "Species richness per cell",
         units         = "Number of species"),
    list(standard_name = "Relative species richness change (Delta_S)",
         long_name     = "Species richness change relative to the previous time step",
         units         = "%"),
    list(standard_name = "Diversity-weighted relative species richness change (Delta_SS)",
         long_name     = "Diversity-weighted relative species richness change",
         units         = "%")
  ),
  scenario = list(
    list(standard_name = "SSP1xRCP2.6 LU",
         long_name     = "Global Sustainability; land-use effects only"),
    list(standard_name = "SSP3xRCP6.0 LU",
         long_name     = "Regional Rivalry; land-use effects only"),
    list(standard_name = "SSP5xRCP8.5 LU",
         long_name     = "Fossil-Fuel Development; land-use effects only")
  ),
  overwrite = TRUE,
  verbose   = FALSE
)




Whichever path you choose, review the final JSON before building the file. Use the portal form or ?ebv_metadata to check controlled vocabulary values; do not invent close-sounding alternatives.
crumbs: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata

title: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata
text:
3.5 Before moving to Unit 4
You now have the information needed to define an EBVCube:

if you are following the tutorial example, you have inspected dataset id = 30 and identified its nine scenario–metric data cubes;
if you are working with your own data, you have checked the spatial layers, entity names, time steps, and creation settings;
in either case, you know how the metadata JSON defines the metrics and scenarios that determine the structure of the file.







Checkpoint. Before continuing, make sure you can explain the difference between the nine data cubes and the 81 spatial slices in dataset id = 30, and identify the metadata JSON, entity names, creation settings, and data values needed to create an EBVCube.
In Unit 4, you will use these components to create the netCDF and populate its data cubes.
crumbs: 3  Preparing biodiversity data and metadata

title: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the ebvcube R package
text:
4.1 Prepare the inputs
The creation workflow requires two main inputs. For this example, both are obtained from the published dataset so that the unit remains self-contained:
The example uses one temporary working folder, so that all files are stored in one place and no step depends on your current working directory. The folder is removed when the R session ends. To keep the files, replace tempdir() with a folder in your project.
# Load ebvcube library
library(ebvcube)

# Keep all files for this example together.
work_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "ebvcube_id30")
dir.create(work_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Download the published source file and define the file we will create.
source_id <- 30L
orig <- ebv_download(id = source_id, outputdir = work_dir, overwrite = FALSE)
new_nc <- file.path(work_dir, "ebvcube_id30_single_cube.nc")

# ebv_download() saves the matching JSON beside the netCDF file.
json <- sub("\\.nc$", "_metadata.json", orig)
stopifnot(file.exists(orig), file.exists(json))

# Read the real structure from the published file so the rebuild lines up.
source_properties <- ebv_properties(orig, verbose = FALSE)
entities <- source_properties@general$entity_names
entities
#> [1] "All birds"  "Forest birds"  "Non-forest birds"
The metadata JSON corresponds to the file generated through Download metadata in the EBV Data Portal. Deriving its path from orig avoids relying on a specific versioned filename.
For your own dataset, create and download the JSON through the portal or generate it in R with ebv_metadata(), as described in Chapter 3.
crumbs: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the `ebvcube` R package

title: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the ebvcube R package
text:
A metadata JSON Describes the dataset, its attributes, metrics, and scenarios. It can be downloaded from the EBV Data Portal or created in R with ebv_metadata().


Data values The spatial values used to populate the data cubes. Here, they are read directly from the published EBVCube.
crumbs: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the `ebvcube` R package

title: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the ebvcube R package
section: 4.2 Create the empty netCDF with ebv_create()
text:
4.2 Create the empty netCDF with ebv_create()
ebv_create() reads the metadata JSON and creates the netCDF structure before any data values are added. You provide the entity names, coordinate reference system, spatial extent, resolution, time steps, and fill value.
For dataset id = 30, the entities are taken directly from the published file so that the reconstructed structure matches the source. The example uses a global 1° grid in EPSG:4326.
The timesteps argument requires particular attention. Dataset id = 30 does not contain a regular annual time series, but three specific years. These are therefore supplied explicitly:

# Create EBVCube with full structure 
ebv_create(
  jsonpath   = json,
  outputpath = new_nc,
  entities   = entities,
  epsg       = 4326,
  extent     = c(-180, 180, -90, 90),
  resolution = c(1, 1),
  timesteps  = c("1900", "2015", "2050"),
  fillvalue  = -3.4e+38,
  overwrite  = TRUE,
  verbose    = FALSE
)

stopifnot(file.exists(new_nc))

At this stage, the EBVCube structure has been created, but no biodiversity data have been added: the data cubes still contain only the fill value. Inspect the file before continuing:

ebv_properties(new_nc, verbose = FALSE)@general$entity_names

ebv_datacubepaths(new_nc, verbose = FALSE)

The entity names should match the values supplied to ebv_create(). Because the metadata JSON defines three scenarios and three metrics, ebv_datacubepaths() should return nine data-cube paths.
If only three paths are returned and they contain no scenario level, check that the scenario information is present in the metadata JSON before continuing. The expected structure was introduced in Chapter 3.
crumbs: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the `ebvcube` R package

title: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the ebvcube R package
section: 4.3 Populate a data cube with ebv_add_data()
text:
4.3 Populate a data cube with ebv_add_data()
Now populate one of the nine data cubes. When scenarios are present, ebv_add_data() uses the scenario, metric, entity, and timestep arguments to determine where the supplied values are written.
For this example, the values come from the published EBVCube itself. We read species richness for Forest birds (entity = 2) under scenario 1 for all three time steps, then write those values to the corresponding cube in the newly created file. type = "a" returns the values as an array suitable for this workflow.

# Define the source slice once and reuse the identifiers in later checks.
source_cube <- "scenario_1/metric_1/ebv_cube"
source_entity <- 2L
source_timesteps <- 1:3  # Positions of 1900, 2015, and 2050 in this file.

# Read one cube from the published dataset.
slice <- ebv_read(orig, source_cube, entity = source_entity,
                  timestep = source_timesteps, type = "a", verbose = FALSE)

# Write it into the matching cube of the reconstructed file.
ebv_add_data(
  filepath_nc = new_nc,
  scenario    = 1,
  metric      = 1,
  entity      = source_entity,
  timestep    = source_timesteps,
  data        = slice,
  verbose     = FALSE
)

For your own dataset, data would contain the values produced by your analysis or model. Depending on your workflow, these can be supplied as an array or from a GeoTIFF. When using a multi-band GeoTIFF, use band to specify which raster bands correspond to the selected time steps.
crumbs: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the `ebvcube` R package

title: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the ebvcube R package
text:
4.4 Verify the reconstructed EBVCube
Before extending the workflow, verify that the values were written correctly. First, use ebv_analyse() to compare simple summaries of the source and reconstructed data:

orig_stats <- ebv_analyse(orig, source_cube, entity = source_entity,
                          verbose = FALSE)
new_stats <- ebv_analyse(new_nc, source_cube, entity = source_entity,
                         verbose = FALSE)

orig_stats[c("mean", "n")]
new_stats[c("mean", "n")]

The mean and number of valid pixels should agree between the two files. This provides a useful summary check, but we can also compare the values directly.

reconstructed_slice <- ebv_read(
  new_nc, source_cube, entity = source_entity,
  timestep = source_timesteps, type = "a", verbose = FALSE
)

isTRUE(all.equal(slice, reconstructed_slice, check.attributes = FALSE))
#> [1] TRUE

A result of TRUE confirms that the values read from the reconstructed cube match the source layers.
The entity identifier must remain consistent throughout the check. We populated Forest birds (entity = 2); the other entities in this cube still contain only fill values.
You can also map one time step as a visual check:

ebv_map(new_nc, source_cube, entity = source_entity, timestep = 3, classes = 5)







Optional: rebuild every cube in the example





To reconstruct the entire published dataset, start from a new empty EBVCube and repeat the same operation for every scenario, metric, and entity.
With three scenarios, three metrics, and three entities, the loop performs 27 writes. Each write supplies all three time steps at once.

# Start from a fresh empty EBVCube for the complete reconstruction.
full_nc <- file.path(work_dir, "ebvcube_id30_full_cubes.nc")
ebv_create(
  jsonpath   = json,
  outputpath = full_nc,
  entities   = entities,
  epsg       = 4326,
  extent     = c(-180, 180, -90, 90),
  resolution = c(1, 1),
  timesteps  = c("1900", "2015", "2050"),
  fillvalue  = -3.4e+38,
  overwrite  = TRUE,
  verbose    = FALSE
)

stopifnot(file.exists(full_nc))

# Fill all nine scenario-metric cubes for all three entities.
for (s in 1:3) {
  for (m in 1:3) {
    for (e in seq_along(entities)) {
      dc <- sprintf("scenario_%d/metric_%d/ebv_cube", s, m)
      ebv_add_data(
        filepath_nc = full_nc,
        scenario    = s, metric = m, entity = e, timestep = 1:3,
        data        = ebv_read(orig, dc, entity = e, timestep = 1:3,
                               type = "a", verbose = FALSE),
        verbose     = FALSE
      )
    }
  }
}

After the loop, use the same verification steps shown above on one or more selected layer, replacing new_nc with full_nc.









Optional: correct metadata with ebv_attribute()





Use ebv_attribute() when an existing EBVCube contains a metadata value that needs to be corrected, such as an incorrect unit or description. There is no need to modify dataset id = 30 simply to demonstrate the function, because its published metadata already describe the data.
The following is a reference pattern. Replace each placeholder with the correct file, level, and value for your own dataset:

ebv_attribute(filepath       = "your_file.nc",
              attribute_name = "units",
              value          = "your corrected unit",
              levelpath      = "scenario_1/metric_1",
              verbose        = FALSE)

The levelpath argument specifies where the attribute is stored. For a file with scenarios, for example: - "scenario_1/metric_1" targets the metric level; - "scenario_1/metric_1/ebv_cube" targets the data cube; - "/" targets the global level.









Optional: create a species-level EBVCube





Use ebv_create_taxonomy() when the entities in your dataset are individual species and taxonomic information should be stored with them. This does not apply to dataset id = 30, whose entities represent bird communities.
Unlike ebv_create(), which receives a vector of entity names, ebv_create_taxonomy() uses a CSV table containing the taxonomy of each entity. Each row represents one species, while columns represent taxonomic ranks from higher to lower levels.



order
family
genus
scientificName




Passeriformes
Corvidae
Corvus
Corvus corone


Passeriformes
Paridae
Parus
Parus major



The final column identifies the entities stored in the EBVCube and must correspond to the species represented by the data.
For interoperability, use Darwin Core terms for taxonomic fields, such as order, family, genus, and scientificName. Where available, you can also include an identifier, such as a GBIF usageKey, to link each species to an established taxonomic backbone.






Row order matters



Your taxonomy CSV must contain one row for each entity in the same order that the entities appear in your data. This ensures that each species is linked to the correct layers in the EBVCube.



# Columns run from the highest rank to the lowest. The last column holds the
# entity names. In practice, this table often comes from a GBIF or Catalogue
# of Life export.
taxonomy <- data.frame(
  order          = c("Passeriformes",   "Apodiformes", "Falconiformes"),
  family         = c("Hirundinidae",    "Apodidae",    "Falconidae"),
  genus          = c("Hirundo",         "Apus",        "Falco"),
  scientificName = c("Hirundo rustica", "Apus apus",   "Falco peregrinus")
)
taxonomy_csv <- file.path(work_dir, "taxonomy.csv")
write.csv(taxonomy, taxonomy_csv, row.names = FALSE)

# Use metadata for a species-level dataset, not the JSON from id = 30.
species_json <- "path/to/species_level_metadata.json"
new_nc_tax <- file.path(work_dir, "species_level_ebvcube.nc")

ebv_create_taxonomy(
  jsonpath   = species_json,
  outputpath = new_nc_tax,
  taxonomy   = taxonomy_csv,
  sep        = ",",
  epsg       = 4326,
  extent     = c(-180, 180, -90, 90),
  resolution = c(1, 1),
  timesteps  = c("1900", "2015", "2050"),
  fillvalue  = -3.4e+38,
  overwrite  = TRUE,
  verbose    = FALSE
)

From here, ebv_add_data() works as it did above. The taxonomy is read-only metadata and does not change how you fill the cubes. See ?ebv_create_taxonomy for accepted column names and separator options.



Finally, inspect the reconstructed file once more:

ebv_properties(new_nc, verbose = FALSE)

ebv_datacubepaths(new_nc, verbose = FALSE)







Optional: inspect the file with Panoply





Panoply is a free NASA application for viewing netCDF and HDF5 files. Open the reconstructed .nc file to inspect its group hierarchy, dimensions, and attributes, or to display a selected data cube as a map.
This provides a useful visual inspection of the file before moving on to validation, without requiring additional R code.









Checkpoint. You created an empty EBVCube with ebv_create(), confirmed its nine scenario–metric data cubes, populated one of them with ebv_add_data(), and verified that the written values match the published source.
You now have a populated .nc file ready for the validation and visualisation steps in Chapter 5.
crumbs: 4  Creating an EBVCube with the `ebvcube` R package

title: 5  Validating and visualising your EBVCube
text:
5.1 Choose the file and slice to inspect
The rendered examples use the tutorial reference dataset (portal ID 30), so that the map and trend are visible in this unit. When validating your own file, replace nc with the path to the EBVCube you created in Chapter 4. The example selects the first available data cube, its first entity, and its final time step. These are choices for inspection, not assumptions about your data: replace them with the cube, entity, and date you want to check.
library(ebvcube)

# Tutorial reference dataset. The download is cached in the temporary folder
# during the render, so it is not requested again when already present.
nc <- ebv_download(id = 30, outputdir = tempdir(), overwrite = FALSE)
#> [1] "Downloading file... Please wait."

# To validate your own file instead, use for example:
# nc <- "path/to/your_ebvcube.nc"

cubes <- ebv_datacubepaths(nc, verbose = FALSE)
props <- ebv_properties(nc, verbose = FALSE)

dc       <- cubes$datacubepaths[1]
entity   <- 1
timestep <- length(props@temporal$dates)
crumbs: 5  Validating and visualising your EBVCube

title: 5  Validating and visualising your EBVCube
text:
5.2 1. Check the structure
ebv_datacubepaths() lists the data cubes stored in the file. A data-cube path represents a scenario and metric combination when scenarios are present. Entities are stored as a dimension within each cube, so check their names separately.

cubes
#>                  datacubepaths scenario_names
#> 1 scenario_1/metric_1/ebv_cube SSP1xRCP2.6 LU
#> 2 scenario_1/metric_2/ebv_cube SSP1xRCP2.6 LU
#> 3 scenario_1/metric_3/ebv_cube SSP1xRCP2.6 LU
#> 4 scenario_2/metric_1/ebv_cube SSP3xRCP6.0 LU
#> 5 scenario_2/metric_2/ebv_cube SSP3xRCP6.0 LU
#> 6 scenario_2/metric_3/ebv_cube SSP3xRCP6.0 LU
#> 7 scenario_3/metric_1/ebv_cube SSP5xRCP8.5 LU
#> 8 scenario_3/metric_2/ebv_cube SSP5xRCP8.5 LU
#> 9 scenario_3/metric_3/ebv_cube SSP5xRCP8.5 LU
#>                                                     metric_names
#> 1                                           Species richness (S)
#> 2                     Relative species richness change (Delta_S)
#> 3 Diversity-weighted relative species richness change (Delta_SS)
#> 4                                           Species richness (S)
#> 5                     Relative species richness change (Delta_S)
#> 6 Diversity-weighted relative species richness change (Delta_SS)
#> 7                                           Species richness (S)
#> 8                     Relative species richness change (Delta_S)
#> 9 Diversity-weighted relative species richness change (Delta_SS)

props@general$entity_names
#> [1] "All birds"        "Forest birds"     "Non-forest birds"
props@spatial$extent
#> [1] -180  180  -90   90
props@temporal$dates
#> [1] "1900-01-01" "2015-01-01" "2050-01-01"

Compare this output with the metadata and source data you prepared. The number of paths should equal the number of scenario–metric combinations you intended to create. For the tutorial reference dataset, that is three scenarios times three metrics, or nine paths. A file without scenarios can correctly have only one path per metric.
Check that the entity names, spatial extent, and dates match what you declared. A missing cube, an unexpected entity name, or an empty time axis is a reason to return to the creation workflow before uploading.
crumbs: 5  Validating and visualising your EBVCube

title: 5  Validating and visualising your EBVCube
text:
5.3 2. Check the values
The file structure can be correct even when a cube contains no usable values. ebv_analyse() summarises the selected slice without requiring you to read the complete cube into memory:

stats <- ebv_analyse(
  nc, dc, entity = entity, timestep = timestep, verbose = FALSE
)
stats[c("min", "mean", "max", "n", "NAs")]
#> $min
#> [1] 2.999974
#> 
#> $mean
#> [1] 197.5901
#> 
#> $max
#> [1] 1004.216
#> 
#> $n
#> [1] 64800
#> 
#> $NAs
#> [1] 48077

n is the number of valid pixels. Compare the minimum, maximum, and mean with the units and expected range of your source data. If n is zero, or all cells are NA, that slice was not populated. A value outside the expected range can indicate a unit mismatch, an unexpected fill value, or an issue in the source raster.
If the data covers a large area, repeat this check for a smaller region that you know well. Use a bounding box or shapefile subset only when you can confirm that it overlaps the cube and uses the same coordinate reference system.
crumbs: 5  Validating and visualising your EBVCube

title: 5  Validating and visualising your EBVCube
text:
5.4 3. Inspect the data visually
Visual checks make spatial and temporal problems easier to spot. They complement the numerical summary above: a plausible mean can still hide data in the wrong place or a sudden change at one date.

Map a slicePlot a trendOptional: make a clearer trend figure


ebv_map() creates a map for one entity and time step. Confirm that the data appears in the expected geographic area and that missing areas are plausible for the dataset.

ebv_map(
  nc, dc, entity = entity, timestep = timestep,
  classes = 5, verbose = FALSE
)








A selected EBVCube data slice for visual validation.






ebv_trend() plots one summary value for each time step and returns those values. Look for a flat line when change is expected, an unexplained jump, or a missing time step. Whether a particular pattern is plausible must be judged against your data and method.

trend_values <- ebv_trend(
  nc, dc, entity = entity, method = "mean", verbose = FALSE
)








Mean value over time for the selected EBVCube entity.



trend_values
#> [1] 191.2065 197.8648 197.5901



If you want a presentation-ready figure, reuse the values returned by ebv_trend() with ggplot2. This is optional and does not add another validation requirement. Install ggplot2 first if it is not already available.

# install.packages("ggplot2")  # run once, only if needed

trend_data <- data.frame(
  date  = props@temporal$dates,
  value = trend_values
)

ggplot2::ggplot(trend_data, ggplot2::aes(date, value)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, colour = "#167A5A") +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2, colour = "#167A5A") +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Mean value over time",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Mean value"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12)










If a custom map looks shifted by 180°



This can happen when a raster uses the [0, 360] longitude convention and you add a [-180, 180] basemap. When creating your own map from ebv_read(), rotate the raster before plotting. This changes the display raster, not the EBVCube file.
r <- ebv_read(nc, dc, entity = entity, timestep = timestep, type = "r")
r <- terra::rotate(r)
crumbs: 5  Validating and visualising your EBVCube

title: 5  Validating and visualising your EBVCube
text:
5.5 4. Compare against your metadata
Read the stored information back from the file and compare it with the metadata JSON or the values supplied through ebv_metadata(). Use the selected data-cube path to include metric-specific information.

cube_props <- ebv_properties(nc, dc, verbose = FALSE)

props@general$title
#> [1] "Global trends in biodiversity (BES-SIM cSAR-iDiv)"
props@general$entity_names
#> [1] "All birds"        "Forest birds"     "Non-forest birds"
props@temporal$dates
#> [1] "1900-01-01" "2015-01-01" "2050-01-01"
cube_props@metric
#> $name
#> [1] "Species richness (S)"
#> 
#> $description
#> [1] "Species richness per cell"
#> 
#> $units
#> [1] "Number of species"

The title, entity names, temporal coverage, metric name, description, and units should agree with the metadata you intend to submit. If you find an incorrect attribute, correct it with ebv_attribute() as described in Chapter 4, then repeat the affected checks.
crumbs: 5  Validating and visualising your EBVCube

title: 5  Validating and visualising your EBVCube
text:
5.6 Pre-upload checklist
Before continuing to the portal, confirm the following:

The data-cube paths contain every scenario–metric combination I intended to create.
The entity names, spatial extent, and dates agree with my metadata and source data.
The selected slices contain valid pixels and values in the expected range.
A map of at least one slice appears in the expected location.
A temporal trend has the expected dates and contains no unexplained gaps or jumps.
The stored title and metric information agree with my metadata JSON.
I repeated the relevant checks after making any correction.







Checkpoint. You have checked the structure, values, visual pattern, and metadata of your EBVCube against the information you prepared. You are now ready to upload the file in Chapter 6.
crumbs: 5  Validating and visualising your EBVCube

title: 6  Uploading a dataset to the EBV Data Portal
text:
6.1 Back to the upload form
The submission uses the same New Upload form you met in Chapter 3. Sign in with your GEO BON account.
If you created the metadata JSON through the portal, reopen your draft under Uploads. The General information and EBV attributes tabs should already contain the information you entered earlier, leaving Data upload to finish.
If you created the metadata JSON in R with ebv_metadata(), start a new upload and complete the portal form before attaching the netCDF. Check that the portal fields describe the same dataset as the metadata and file you validated.
crumbs: 6  Uploading a dataset to the EBV Data Portal

title: 6  Uploading a dataset to the EBV Data Portal
text:
6.2 Uploading your netCDF
The Data upload tab offers two ways to submit: a ZIP of GeoTIFFs or a netCDF built with the ebvcube package. You built the netCDF, so choose that option and upload your .nc file.






Add a preview image



The portal accepts a JPG or PNG preview image. A small map of a single slice exported from ebv_map() is a clear choice and makes your dataset easier to recognise in the catalogue. If the portal flags a problem with the submission, return to the checks in Chapter 5, correct the relevant file or metadata, and upload the revised file.
crumbs: 6  Uploading a dataset to the EBV Data Portal

title: 6  Uploading a dataset to the EBV Data Portal
text:
6.3 Submitting for review
Once the file is attached, review the submission and select Submit for review. In Draft mode, the person who submitted the dataset has editing rights. Submitting confirms that the dataset is ready for review; use any feedback from that process to identify whether the metadata, netCDF file, or both need revision.
Published datasets appear in the public catalogue and can be downloaded with ebv_download().
crumbs: 6  Uploading a dataset to the EBV Data Portal

title: 6  Uploading a dataset to the EBV Data Portal
section: 6.4 After publication: DOI, citation, and versions
text:
6.4 After publication: DOI, citation, and versions
On publication, the portal page displays the dataset DOI and citation. You can see these on the live page for the running example, dataset ID 30, together with its version history.






Cite the dataset, not the package



Use the dataset DOI when citing your data — not the ebvcube package citation, which credits the software rather than the dataset. If you later revise the data, use the portal’s versioning workflow and keep the netCDF file, metadata JSON, and description of the changes together. This preserves a clear record of what each version represents.





If the page does not load, open dataset ID 30 on the EBV Data Portal.







Checkpoint. Your validated netCDF is attached to a portal submission, and you know how to submit it for review. After publication, use the dataset page to find its DOI, citation, and version information. If anything snagged along the way, Chapter 7 collects the fixes for the problems that come up most often.
crumbs: 6  Uploading a dataset to the EBV Data Portal

title: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help
text:
7.1 Installing the package
These problems can prevent library(ebvcube) from loading. Return to Chapter 2 for the full installation steps.
crumbs: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help

title: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help
text:
A Bioconductor package is not found





An error such as there is no package called 'rhdf5', DelayedArray, or HDF5Array means that a required Bioconductor dependency is unavailable. Install the dependencies, then restart R and try loading ebvcube again:

install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install(c("rhdf5", "DelayedArray", "HDF5Array"))

library(ebvcube)

If BiocManager is already installed, the first line can be skipped. It selects the Bioconductor release that is compatible with your R version.









package ‘ebvcube’ is not available for this version of R





First check the installed R version:

R.version.string

ebvcube requires R 4.2.0 or later. Update R if the installed version is older, then repeat the installation in Chapter 2. If updating R is not possible, use a package version documented as compatible with your R version; check the package release notes before selecting a version.









Installation fails on Linux with HDF5, GDAL, or PROJ errors





This can indicate that the system libraries required by rhdf5 or terra are missing. On Debian or Ubuntu, install the libraries from a terminal:
sudo apt-get install libhdf5-dev libgdal-dev libproj-dev libgeos-dev libudunits2-dev
Then reinstall the dependency named in the error message, rather than only reinstalling ebvcube. Package names and installation commands differ on other Linux distributions; use the equivalent packages supplied by that distribution.









HDF5 library version mismatched





An HDF5 library version mismatched error can occur when rhdf5 was built against a different HDF5 library from the one loaded by R. Close all R sessions, start a clean session, and reinstall rhdf5:

remove.packages("rhdf5")
BiocManager::install("rhdf5", force = TRUE)

Then restart R once more and retry the operation.
crumbs: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help

title: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help
text:
7.2 Preparing data and metadata
Problems at this stage usually concern controlled vocabulary values or inputs that do not describe the same dataset. The complete preparation workflow is in Chapter 3.






A metadata value is rejected





Fields such as ebv_class, ebv_name, and ebv_entity_type accept controlled vocabulary values. If ebv_metadata() or the portal form rejects a value, compare it with the available options in the portal form or the accepted values in ?ebv_metadata. Use the listed wording rather than a close alternative.









The metadata, rasters, and creation settings do not agree





Before creating the file, confirm that the spatial layers have a common coordinate reference system, extent, and resolution; that their ordering matches the entity names and time steps; and that the metadata JSON describes the same metrics and scenarios. These checks prevent most dimension and indexing problems during cube creation.
crumbs: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help

title: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help
text:
7.3 Creating the cube
Errors here often indicate that the metadata, creation settings, and supplied data do not describe the same dimensions. See Chapter 4 for the complete workflow.






entities length does not match metadata





ebv_create() requires one entity name for each entity declared by the metadata JSON. Compare the vector you supplied with the metadata, then correct the vector or JSON so their entity counts agree. Keep the entity order consistent with the order of the data supplied later.









ebv_add_data() fails with a dimension mismatch





This error can occur when the raster does not match the target cube’s coordinate reference system, resolution, extent, or number of layers. Read one target slice to use as a grid template, then align the input raster before adding it:

target_r <- ebv_read(
  new_nc, "scenario_1/metric_1/ebv_cube",
  entity = 1, timestep = 1, type = "r", verbose = FALSE
)

r <- terra::rast("your_data.tif")
r_aligned <- terra::project(r, target_r)
terra::writeRaster(r_aligned, "your_data_aligned.tif", overwrite = TRUE)

Replace the data-cube path, entity, and time step with a valid target in your file. Before calling ebv_add_data(), also check that the raster layers correspond to the time steps you provide.









Units, titles, or descriptions are incorrect after ebv_create()





Correct the affected attribute with ebv_attribute(), as shown in Chapter 4, then repeat the relevant checks in Chapter 5. Rebuilding the netCDF is not required solely to correct an attribute.
crumbs: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help

title: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help
text:
7.4 Reading and validating the file
These issues can occur while checking your own file or reading a published EBVCube. The standard validation checks are in Chapter 5.






ebv_read() reports “Not enough RAM”





The selected cube or slice is larger than the available memory limit. Reduce the amount read by using ebv_read_bb() for a bounding box or ebv_read_shp() for a polygon, or use type = "da" to work with a DelayedArray on disk. ignore_RAM = TRUE disables the package’s safety check; it does not reduce the amount of memory a normal read requires.









ebv_read_shp() returns only NA values





First check whether the polygon overlaps the cube’s extent. If it does, compare its coordinate reference system with a raster read from the cube. Reproject the polygon to the target raster’s CRS before saving it and trying the subset again:

target_r <- ebv_read(nc, dc, entity = 1, timestep = 1, type = "r",
                     verbose = FALSE)
shp_aligned <- sf::st_transform(sf::st_read(shp), terra::crs(target_r))
sf::st_write(shp_aligned, "shp_aligned.shp", delete_dsn = TRUE)

terra::ext(target_r)
sf::st_bbox(shp_aligned)

The final two lines provide the two extents for comparison. Use the saved, aligned shapefile in ebv_read_shp() only when the extents overlap.









The map appears shifted by 180°





This can occur when the raster uses longitudes from [0, 360] and a basemap uses [-180, 180]. When creating a custom map from ebv_read(), rotate the display raster before plotting:

r <- ebv_read(nc, dc, entity = entity, timestep = timestep, type = "r")
r <- terra::rotate(r)

This changes the raster used for display, not the EBVCube file.
crumbs: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help

title: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help
text:
7.5 Uploading to the portal
The submission steps are in Chapter 6. Use the portal’s validation feedback to identify whether the file, metadata, or submission information needs attention.






The upload is rejected or does not complete





Run the checklist in Chapter 5 again and correct any reported issue before uploading a revised file. Confirm that the file and portal fields refer to the same dataset and that the upload has finished before leaving the page. If the problem continues after a successful local validation, record the portal message, the time of the attempt, and the dataset draft or submission identifier, then contact the portal team through the dataset page or GEO BON contact route.









A value is not available in a portal list





The portal lists the values it accepts for controlled fields. Select a term only when it accurately describes the dataset. If none of the available terms fits, ask the portal team for guidance rather than substituting an inaccurate value or editing the metadata to bypass the form.









The dataset remains in review





Review requires action by the portal team and may result in a request for changes. Check the submission page and the email address associated with the account for feedback. If there has been no update after a reasonable review period, contact the portal team with the dataset identifier and submission date.
crumbs: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help

title: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help
text:
7.6 Working with large files






Reads are slow from a network drive





netCDF/HDF5 files can require many small reads. A network drive can add delay to each one. Where your data-handling policy permits it, copy the file to a local working directory before reading it:

local_nc <- file.path(tempdir(), basename(nc))
file.copy(nc, local_nc, overwrite = TRUE)

Use local_nc for the read, while retaining the original file unchanged.









Plotting a full-resolution raster is slow





For an exploratory map, read a selected slice and aggregate it before plotting. Choose a factor that retains the geographic pattern needed for the check:

r <- ebv_read(nc, dc, entity = entity, timestep = timestep, type = "r")
r_small <- terra::aggregate(r, fact = 4, fun = "mean")
plot(r_small)

Use the original-resolution data for the final analysis or export when required.
crumbs: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help

title: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help
text:
7.7 Keep a recoverable workflow






Before and after each correction



Keep a copy of the metadata JSON, the netCDF you validated before upload, and the script used to create the file. Record what you changed, then repeat the relevant validation checks in Chapter 5. When referring to a published dataset, cite its DOI from the portal page; use citation("ebvcube") when citing the software itself.
crumbs: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help

title: 7  Troubleshooting and getting help
text:
7.8 Getting help and reporting bugs
If the entries above do not resolve the problem, first identify whether it occurs in the package or in the portal. Report package errors through the GitHub issue tracker. For a question about using the package, use GitHub Discussions. For a portal upload, review, or metadata-form issue, use the portal contact route.
A report is easier to investigate when it includes:

the complete error message;
the output of sessionInfo() and packageVersion("ebvcube");
a minimal reproducible example, where possible; and
the result you expected and the result you observed.

Do not include data that you are not permitted to share. If the problem has already been fixed in a newer release, updating the package may resolve it; check the installed version before posting.






Checkpoint. You can identify the stage where a problem occurred, apply the relevant check or correction, and collect the information needed for further help. For additional documentation and references, see Chapter 8.

title: 8  Further reading and references
text:
8.1 Package documentation and source code
For function-level details, use the ebvcube function reference. The source repository contains the package code, release history, and the package citation (Quoss et al., 2024).
The released package is available from CRAN. The B-Cubed r-universe package collection also lists ebvcube and may provide more recent builds. When reproducibility matters, record the version returned by packageVersion("ebvcube").
For installation and a first working example, return to Chapter 2. For creating, reading, or mapping an EBVCube, the package documentation is the best next step after the relevant tutorial unit.
crumbs: 8  Further reading and references

title: 8  Further reading and references
section: 8.2 Format standards and the EBV framework
text:
8.2 Format standards and the EBV framework
The EBVCube netCDF format specification is the authoritative description of the file structure, required attributes, and metadata conventions. Consult it when a question concerns the contents of the netCDF file rather than how to use an R function.
The format builds on the CF Metadata Conventions and the Attribute Convention for Data Discovery (ACDD) (Earth Science Information Partners, 2015; Eaton et al., 2020). For the broader scientific context, see GEO BON’s introduction to Essential Biodiversity Variables and the foundational EBV paper (Pereira et al., 2013).
crumbs: 8  Further reading and references

title: 8  Further reading and references
section: 8.3 The EBV Data Portal and the tutorial dataset
text:
8.3 The EBV Data Portal and the tutorial dataset
Use the EBV Data Portal to discover published datasets, view their metadata, and begin a submission. The dataset page for Global trends in biodiversity (BES-SIM cSAR-iDiv) is the running example used in this tutorial. It provides the dataset metadata, available downloads, and its official citation (Martins & Pereira, 2022).
When referring to that published dataset, cite its DOI: 10.25829/5zmy41. Do not cite the package in place of the dataset. The package and the EBVCube design are described in the methods paper (Quoß et al., 2022).
For the complete submission workflow, return to Chapter 6. If a file is not ready to upload, repeat the checks in Chapter 5 before creating or updating a portal submission.
crumbs: 8  Further reading and references

title: 8  Further reading and references
text:
8.4 Getting help and reporting problems
For a reproducible package error or a feature request, open an issue in the ebvcube GitHub issue tracker. For a question about how to use the package, begin with the function reference and troubleshooting guide; if you need to open an issue, include the error message, sessionInfo(), the installed package version, and a minimal reproducible example where possible.
For a portal upload, metadata-form, review, or dataset-specific problem, use the contact route provided by the portal. The troubleshooting guide in Chapter 7 will help you identify whether the issue belongs with the package or the portal before you ask for help.






Checkpoint. You can now locate the documentation and specification that match your task, find the appropriate support route, and cite both the software and the dataset used in your work. All external links in this unit were checked on 1 September 2026.
